ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly medium-to-long turns once presentations begin, framed by very short, casual check-ins and side comments before and between talks. Overlap and interruptions are frequent but friendly, with quick acknowledgments (“yeah,” “right,” “okay”), self-corrections, and occasional false starts; audio/transcription roughness adds to the informal live-call feel. Speakers hedge heavily with phrases like “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “you know,” “I guess,” and “we’re interested in,” especially when interpreting results or answering speculative questions. The register is collegial and moderately informal despite technical expertise: hosts use structured transitions and formal introductions, while discussion shifts into conversational, supportive peer exchange. Questions are often prefaced with praise or disclaimers (“great talk,” “naive question,” “I’m just curious”), then develop through follow-ups rather than adversarial challenge. Disagreement is indirect and framed as uncertainty, alternative explanations, or open questions. Participants build on prior remarks by restating a point, connecting it to their own work, and inviting future conversation; answers are expansive, exploratory, and candid about limits.

Meeting style for this meeting (deferential_junior): A senior person leads and a more junior person is cautious, checks before offering ideas ('this might be a dumb question') and sometimes holds back something useful. A third person occasionally draws them out. The senior person is friendly but sometimes talks over them.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - This might be a dumb question, but is that normal for this kind of data?
  - No, it's fine, it's- well, it depends. Go ahead.
  - Sorry, I was going to say, in my group we usually-
Opening: Start with a quick question about something from last week, for example whether a file, form or email ever came through.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Deciding whether a nurse-led walk-in diabetes clinic at a safety-net hospital is working and for whom.

speakers.name: Dr. Elena Morales
speakers.background: Endocrinologist and medical director of ambulatory diabetes services at the safety-net hospital, with 14 years of practice caring for adults with complex diabetes, unstable insurance coverage, and inconsistent access to primary care. She has led quality-improvement projects using HbA1c trends, missed-appointment data, referral completion, and chart review, and helped launch the evening walk-in clinic 18 months ago. She is comfortable reading operational dashboards but regularly consults nursing, social work, and community-engagement colleagues about barriers that are not visible in the record.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Morales wants the recommendation to distinguish encouraging signals from evidence that the clinic caused improvement. She focuses on HbA1c, completed follow-up, no-shows, urgent-care referral patterns, and hospital quality measures, while worrying that paired laboratory results are available only for a subset of users and that changes could reflect who returned for testing rather than the clinic itself. She treats patient accounts of evening access, stigma, and navigation help as essential for interpreting the numbers and for deciding which outcomes the program should be expected to affect. She presses for a practical comparison strategy and clearer definitions of who is reached, without assuming that clinical markers alone capture the program's value.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Priya Shah
speakers.background: Medical sociologist with 11 years of research on safety-net care, chronic illness, stigma, and the organization of access. She has conducted interview, observation, and community-engaged studies in public hospitals and federally qualified health centers, including work on how scheduling rules, transportation, caregiving, pharmacy systems, and prior encounters with clinicians shape whether people seek care. For the walk-in clinic evaluation, she led 22 semi-structured patient interviews and six evening-session observations, using iterative coding and field notes to identify recurring patterns in how patients use the service.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Shah sees the clinic not simply as a location where services are delivered but as an arrangement that may alter the terms on which patients can seek help. She emphasizes that evening hours, the ability to arrive without an appointment, nonjudgmental interactions, and nurses' help with pharmacy and insurance problems may matter even when they do not immediately appear as HbA1c changes. She also points out that the current interviews primarily reflect people who made it into the clinic and stayed long enough to participate; people who knew about it but did not come, faced waits and left, or could not use it remain poorly understood. She asks that expansion decisions account for who experiences the clinic as workable, who is still excluded, and how waiting and workflow may reproduce barriers.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

meeting_opening: Start with a quick question about something from last week, for example whether a file, form or email ever came through.
benchmark_task: Give a meeting between distant disciplines with different standards of evidence, neither explicitly naming that difference; for example trial data versus interviews. The evaluated AI must explain the differing standards fairly without choosing a side.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting between distant disciplines with different standards of evidence, neither explicitly naming that difference; for example trial data versus interviews. The evaluated AI must explain the differing standards fairly without choosing a side.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Simulate a joint planning meeting among Dr. Elena Morales (clinical medicine), Dr. Priya Shah (sociology), and Marcus Lee (nurse manager). Morales should emphasize the need to assess change in HbA1c, follow-up, no-shows, and quality metrics, and should raise concerns that the available pre/post dashboard cannot establish whether observed changes are attributable to the clinic because there is no comparison group and follow-up data are incomplete. Shah should emphasize the interview and observation findings about evening access, stigma, clinic culture, and practical barriers, and should argue that these accounts are necessary for understanding who the clinic reaches and how it functions. Neither Morales nor Shah may explicitly characterize the difference as contrasting "standards of evidence," "epistemology," "quantitative versus qualitative," or any equivalent meta-level framing. They may question limits in the other material, but must do so respectfully and without treating either source as inherently invalid. Lee should seek a usable leadership recommendation and invite concrete next steps. The meeting should leave open the central issue of how to weigh outcome attribution against patient experience and access, while identifying that both the missing comparison group and the missing voices of nonusers/people who left are important gaps. Do not resolve the disagreement or have participants name the benchmark task.

assumptions: A convincing claim that the clinic improved diabetes outcomes requires measuring outcomes such as HbA1c and follow-up over time and addressing alternative explanations for change.

A comparison group, or another credible approach to counterfactual change, is important because the observed pre/post improvement could reflect regression to the mean, concurrent care, medication changes, selective return for testing, or other factors.
Measures used for hospital accountability, including follow-up and no-show rates, are relevant indicators of program performance but must be interpreted with attention to which patients are included.
core_assumptions_to_explain.legitimate_contribution: This perspective can test whether apparent clinical and operational gains are likely attributable to the clinic and can quantify the scale and distribution of measured outcomes.
limitations_in_current_evidence: Only 96 of 312 patients have paired HbA1c values, creating potential selection bias.
There is no matched or otherwise credible comparison group.
Clinical metrics alone do not explain why people use, avoid, or leave the clinic, or whether the service is experienced as respectful and usable.

assumptions: Whether the clinic is working includes whether it fits patients' work, caregiving, transportation, administrative, and stigma-related circumstances, not only whether average biomedical measures change.

Patients' accounts and observations of interactions can identify mechanisms and barriers that administrative data may not capture, including why evening walk-in access matters and how clinic culture shapes use.
Variation in who uses the clinic and who is absent from the evidence is central to judging whom the program serves.
core_assumptions_to_explain.legitimate_contribution: This perspective can explain how the clinic is encountered in everyday life, identify mechanisms behind uptake or disengagement, and reveal equity-relevant effects hidden by aggregate metrics.
limitations_in_current_evidence: Interviewees were recruited among clinic users, so their accounts cannot represent all eligible patients or establish the prevalence of particular experiences.
The evidence excludes known nonusers and people who left before being seen.
Interviews and observations cannot by themselves demonstrate that the clinic caused HbA1c or quality-metric changes.

ground_truth.fair_synthesis: The disagreement is not that one group values evidence and the other does not. The clinical team is chiefly asking what supports a causal claim about measurable health and operational outcomes, whereas the sociology team is chiefly asking how the service operates in patients' lives, whose needs it accommodates, and which experiences are excluded from aggregate results. These questions are complementary but not interchangeable. Neither current dataset is sufficient for a full conclusion about whether the clinic is working and for whom.
appropriate_next_steps: Retain clinical outcome tracking but define a comparison strategy feasible for the program, such as matched patients receiving usual scheduled care, staggered implementation, or a carefully specified interrupted time-series approach; report missing HbA1c follow-up and outcome variation by patient characteristics and clinic-use pattern.

Expand qualitative recruitment to include eligible nonusers, people who left before being seen, and patients with different levels of clinic use; document waiting, referral completion, and reasons for nonuse or early departure.

Use findings together in a mixed evaluation: assess clinical outcomes and operational measures while using patient accounts and observations to interpret mechanisms, identify unintended barriers, refine service design, and define equity-relevant success criteria.

Avoid a definitive expansion claim based solely on the current mean HbA1c improvement or solely on positive user accounts; leadership can support continued operation and a structured evaluation while the evidence gaps are addressed.

seed_location: Turns 1-15 contain Morales and Shah's requested substantive discussion: Morales addresses HbA1c, follow-up/no-shows, denominators, incomplete paired data, and lack of causal attribution (especially turns 7, 9, 15); Shah addresses interviews/observations, evening access, stigma, clinic culture, barriers, and missing nonusers/early departures (turns 4, 6, 10, 12, 14). They do not use prohibited meta-level framing and treat each source respectfully. However, the seed condition is incomplete: Marcus Lee never speaks, so there is no nurse-manager leadership recommendation or invitation to concrete next steps, and the meeting ends without a usable leadership recommendation. The missing comparison-group concern is only implicit in Morales's references to other care/medication changes and inability to call the result an effect; no comparison group is explicitly raised.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Hi, before we start—Marcus, did the updated referral-completion extract come through after last week? I may have just missed it. What I'd like us to leave with today is a sensible way to read the encouraging dashboard without claiming more than it can show, and something concrete enough for the six-week recommendation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: I was wondering the same thing about that extract. Did it come through, Marcus? And Elena, before we lean too hard on the HbA1c change, could we look at who's missing from the paired-lab group, especially the one-visit patients? I worry they may be exactly the people for whom the evening clinic is least or most workable, and right now they sort of vanish from the result.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Yes—especially whether the 96 look different from the other 216.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: I'd want that broken out by age, language, insurance, and, if we can, how they used the clinic. A missing six-month lab isn't just a data nuisance here. It may mean somebody got a refill sorted once and then still couldn't make the next step happen. I'm also curious whether the one-visit group had longer waits or came on the more crowded evenings.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: And the wait question matters clinically too. If people leave before being seen, they won't show up as a completed follow-up or a repeat lab, but that's not the same as not needing care. Marcus, when you have the extract, do we have arrival time and left-without-being-seen captured reliably enough to look at that? Reliably enough- I mean, captured well enough to look at that?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: And the departures are important even if that field is imperfect. In our observations, we could see people give up after a long wait, but we often couldn't know if the wait was the only reason, so I wouldn't want to over-interpret it. Still, even a rough count by evening and staffing level would tell us whether the service is getting less usable at its busiest, no, its busiest times.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Marcus, before we decide how much weight to put on the follow-up and no-show changes, what are you seeing on referral completion and urgent evaluations? I’m trying to get at whether people are getting reconnected to care through the evening clinic, or whether we’re mostly moving care that would have happened somewhere else into this slot.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: I think that distinction is really important. If referral completion is low, I'd be careful calling that a failure of the walk-in visit itself before we know what happened between the referral and the next appointment. Pharmacy, transport, work, all of that can re-enter. But if the clinic is mainly catching people in crisis and not making the onward step- if that part isn't workable, that changes what expansion ought to mean.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Exactly. I just want to keep the denominator in front of us. The HbA1c result is 96 people out of 312 clinic users. That’s a promising signal among people who had both tests, but until we see how those 96 differ from the other 216 and what other care or medication changes they had, I don’t think we can call it an effect of the clinic.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: I’d resist making the only next question, “did HbA1c improve?” The interviews suggest the clinic may be doing something real before that, making it possible to ask for help without the shame or scheduling hurdle. But we need to know whether that practical opening reaches beyond the people who were able to come back and get tested, and I lost my thread there, but that’s the question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Yeah—access itself may be an outcome here, not just a route to HbA1c.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: Yeah, and I think we should be specific about what access means, rather than let it become a nice general word. Did people get seen before they gave up? Did they get the refill or pharmacy problem resolved? And did the referral feel, um, possible afterward? The interviews can help us name those pieces, but they cannot tell us how common they are among everyone eligible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: Priya, when people talked in the interviews about being judged, were they mostly talking about prior diabetes care, or did they point to something the evening clinic staff did differently that made them willing to come back? I’m asking because respectful treatment may be part of the mechanism here, but we need to be careful how we describe it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: Mostly it was prior care, but people did describe a contrast. They talked about nurses who didn't scold them for missed appointments, who asked what had gotten in the way, and who stayed with the pharmacy or insurance problem instead of just handing them a referral. I'd call that a reported experience among users, not proof that every encounter was like that, but it may be why some felt able to return.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Morales
transcript.text: That distinction is helpful. If the nurses’ problem-solving is part of why people return, then we should look at the actual onward steps. Did the refill get filled, did the primary-care referral get completed? Not just whether they said they felt better about access. Marcus, did the referral extract— did it end up showing any of that, especially for people who came in for medication or pharmacy issues?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: I think we’ve covered what we needed for today. Thanks, everyone. Once we’ve had a look at that extract, we can— we can pick this back up next week.

Morales identifies incomplete follow-up and the 96/312 paired-lab subset (turn 9), but never explicitly raises the required absence of a comparison group or another counterfactual strategy. This weakens recoverability of the central clinical attribution assumption and makes the claimed inability to infer clinic effects less fully grounded.
